deep_dive_html:
In the high-stakes world of medical real estate, the Common Area Maintenance (CAM) clause is often the most significant driver of unbudgeted operational costs. Landlords frequently draft these provisions with broad, ambiguous language designed to pass through virtually any property-related cost to the tenant.

The Danger of Capital Expenditure Pass-Throughs

A primary vulnerability for medical practices lies in the inclusion of capital improvements within the definition of operating expenses. While routine maintenance is a standard tenant obligation, landlords often attempt to include the cost of structural replacements—such as new HVAC systems, parking lot resurfacing, or roof replacements—under the guise of maintenance. For a medical practice, these sudden, massive assessments can disrupt cash flow and jeopardize the stability of the practice.

  • Undefined Administrative Fees: Landlords may charge arbitrary management fees that are not tied to actual costs.
  • Uncapped Controllable Expenses: Without a cap, the landlord has no incentive to manage costs efficiently.
  • Lack of Audit Rights: Without the ability to verify expense statements, tenants are forced to accept whatever the landlord presents.

Establishing Market-Standard Protections

To protect your practice, your lease must distinguish between controllable and non-controllable expenses. A sophisticated negotiation focuses on three pillars of protection:

  • The Expense Cap: Negotiating a fixed percentage cap on the year-over-year increase of controllable operating expenses.
  • Capital Expenditure Exclusion: Explicitly stating that any item qualifying as a capital improvement must be amortized over its useful life.
  • The Right to Audit: Ensuring the tenant has the contractual right to inspect the landlord's books and records related to CAM charges.
